What is the structure of your dataset?¶

There are 183412 records in the dataset with 16 features/columns duration_sec, start_time, end_time, start_station_id, start_station_name, start_station_longitude, start_station_latitude, end_station_name, end_station_latitude, end_station_longitude, bike_id, user_type, member_birth_year, member_gender, now there are 174952 records after handling the missing values

What is/are the main feature(s) of interest in your dataset?¶

I'm interested in looking how trip duration(duration_sec) dependent on user type, start station, end station, member gender, age

What features in the dataset do you think will help support your investigation into your feature(s) of interest?¶

I think the trip duration(duration_sec) feature of dataset will support my investigation on features like start_station, end_station, gender, age, and user_type can support my investigation

Univariate Exploration¶

Ques:1 Which type of users use the bike sharing system most?¶

In [12]:
#plotting the user type distribution using the countplot
plt.figure(figsize=(7,5))

sb.countplot(data=new_df, x='user_type', edgecolor='black')
plt.title('Distribution of User Type', fontsize=14)
plt.xlabel('User Type')
plt.ylabel('Count')

ax = plt.gca()
for container in ax.containers :
    ax.bar_label(container)

plt.show()

Observation

  • Most of the riders are Subsribers than Customers
  • Riders are the regular customers who have became the permanent Subscribers

Ques:2 Which type of gender use the bike sharing system most?¶

In [13]:
#plotting the gender distribution using the countplot
plt.figure(figsize=(7,5))

sb.countplot(data=new_df, x='member_gender', edgecolor='black')
plt.title('Distribution of Member', fontsize=14)
plt.xlabel('Gender')
plt.ylabel('Count')

ax = plt.gca()
for container in ax.containers :
    ax.bar_label(container)

plt.show()

Observation

  • Male riders dominate the dataset
  • Female riders are comparetively fewer
  • The other category has shown very few number of representation
  • This shows the gender imbalance in the dataset

Quest3: How are trip durations distributed among users?¶

In [14]:
#We will show the distribution of the trip duration
plt.figure(figsize=(7,5))

#need to explicitly define the the bins range
bin_size=700
bins = np.arange(0, df['duration_sec'].max()+bin_size, bin_size)
plt.hist(new_df['duration_sec'], bins=bins, edgecolor='black')

# adding title and labels
plt.title('Trip Duration Distribution')
plt.xlabel('Duration (Seconds)')
plt.ylabel('Frequency')
plt.axis([-500,8000, 0, 130000])
plt.show()

Observation

  • Most trips are short-duration rides i.e [0-700 sec]
  • Distribution is heavily right-skewed.
  • Few trips have extremely long durations.

Discuss the distribution(s) of your variable(s) of interest. Were there any unusual points? Did you need to perform any transformations?¶

The trip duration distribution was highly right-skewed, where most rides were concentrated within shorter durations. Subscribers contributed the majority of rides, while male riders used the service more frequently than other genders. Most riders belonged to the 20–40 age group, and only a few start and end stations handled most of the bike traffic.

Of the features you investigated, were there any unusual distributions? Did you perform any operations on the data to tidy, adjust, or change the form of the data? If so, why did you do this?¶

Birth year was transformed into age for easier demographic analysis and interpretation. In addition, np.arange() was used in histogram bins to create cleaner and more readable visualizations.

Bivariate Exploration¶

1. Age vs Trip Duration¶

Question: Does age affect the trip duration?

In [18]:
#plotting the age vs trip duration using scatterplot
plt.figure(figsize=(10,6))

sb.scatterplot(data=new_df, x='age', y='duration_sec', alpha=0.2)
plt.xlabel('Age')
plt.ylabel('Duration(Sec)')
plt.title('Trip Duration vs Age')
plt.axis([10,100, -500, 10500])

plt.show()

Observation

  • Most riders are between the ages of 20–40, showing that younger adults use the bike service more frequently.
  • Younger riders tend to have longer trip durations, while older riders generally take shorter trips.
  • The relationship between age and trip duration is weakly negative, as long-duration trips decrease with increasing age.

2. User Type vs Trip Duration¶

Question: Does user type affect the trip duration?

In [19]:
# calculating average trip duration by user type
avg_duration = new_df.groupby('user_type')['duration_sec'].mean().reset_index()
plt.figure(figsize=(10,6))

sb.barplot(data=avg_duration, x='user_type', y='duration_sec', hue='user_type')
plt.xlabel('User Type')
plt.ylabel('Duration(Sec)')
plt.title('Trip Duration vs User Type')

ax = plt.gca()
for container in ax.containers :
    ax.bar_label(container)
    
plt.show()

Observation

  • The plot shows the average trip duration for each user type.
  • Customers have a higher average trip duration compared to Subscribers.
  • This indicates that Customers generally take longer trips, while Subscribers tend to take shorter rides.

3. Gender vs Trip Duration¶

Does trip duration vary across genders?

In [39]:
# calculating average trip duration by gender
avg_gender_duration = new_df.groupby('member_gender')['duration_sec'].mean().reset_index()
# plotting clustered bar chart
plt.figure(figsize=(8,5))
sb.barplot(data=avg_gender_duration, x='member_gender', y='duration_sec')
plt.title('Average Trip Duration vs Gender')
plt.xlabel('Gender')
plt.ylabel('Average Trip Duration (Seconds)')

plt.show()

Observation

  • Average trip durations are relatively similar across different gender categories.
  • Male riders contribute the highest number of trips overall.
  • Slight variation in trip duration exists between gender groups.

4. Start Station vs Trip Duration¶

Does trip duration vary across different Start Stations?

In [38]:
#selecting top 10 start stations
top_start = new_df['start_station_name'].value_counts().head(10).index
#now filtering the dataset 
start_df = new_df[new_df['start_station_name'].isin(top_start)]

Q1 = start_df['duration_sec'].quantile(0.25)
Q3 = start_df['duration_sec'].quantile(0.75)
IQR = Q3 - Q1 

lower = Q1 - 1.5 * IQR
upper = Q3 - 1.5 * IQR

start_df

plt.ylabel('Start Station Name')
plt.title('Start Station vs Trip Duration')

plt.show()

Observation

  • Trip Durations are fairly consistent among all the trip durations
  • Some start stations have high median trip durations

Talk about some of the relationships you observed in this part of the investigation. Were there features that strengthened each other in terms of looking at your feature(s) of interest?¶

Trip durations are influenced by demographic and trip related features. Customers generally took longer rides than Subscribers across different age groups and gender categories. while most riders remains shorter regardless of rider age

Were there any interesting or surprising interactions between features?¶

Although the customers and male riders contributes the maximum number of trips, they mostly shows the shorted ride durations.

Conclusions¶

The univariate analysis showed that most bike rides were short-duration trips, indicating that the bike-sharing system is mainly used for daily commuting. Subscribers contributed the highest number of rides, male riders dominated the dataset, and most users belonged to the 20–40 age group. The start and end station analysis also showed that only a few stations handled most of the bike traffic.

The bivariate analysis revealed that user type had the strongest relationship with trip duration, where Customers generally took longer rides than Subscribers. Age showed only a weak relationship with trip duration, while trip duration patterns across genders remained relatively similar. Start and end stations also showed noticeable variation in ride durations.

The multivariate analysis further showed that Customers consistently took longer rides across different age groups and gender categories, while Subscribers mainly used the service for shorter commuting trips.

Steps included :

  1. Performed Preliminary Wrangling were we load the dataset and look on the top 5 values, identified the datatypes of the columsns according interest of exploration, then performed data cleaning handle the missing values and outliers
  2. Next moved to univariate exploration where every features are explored individually for insight and patterns and identified the observations.
  3. In bivariate and multivariate exploration every feature is looked upon with the trip duration which helps in understanding the primary relationship between all targeted features with duration_sec(trip duration)
